passages.no: The fourth year of King Xi of Yan, 251 BC; the text calls him "the present king" (今王). 四战之国: the Zhengyi: Zhao borders Yan to the east, Qin to the west, Han and Wei to the south and the Hu and Mo to the north, hence "at war on four sides". The Suoyin: five men against one. The Suoyin and the Zhengyi cite the Zhanguoce, which differs: Lian Po met Li Fu at Hao with two hundred thousand men, Yue Cheng met Qing Qin at Dai with fifty thousand, and the men of Yan were heavily defeated. The Zhanguoce writes the general's name 爰秦 (Suoyin) or 庆秦 (Zhengyi). The Suoyin: Zhao wished to have Jiang Qu put in charge of making the peace; the Jijie: Yan made Jiang Qu its Chancellor. The twelfth year of King Kaolie of Chu, 251 BC. The fifteenth year of King Xiaocheng of Zhao, 251 BC. 尉文: the Suoyin: probably a place name, or else 尉 an office and 文 a name, the grant being the land that Wen had held; the Zhengyi: probably land in Weizhou. The Hereditary House of Yan, above, has Yue Jian flee to Zhao. The twenty-sixth year of King Anxi of Wei, 251 BC. The twenty-second year of King Huanhui of Han, 251 BC. The entries of the Hereditary Houses for this year: the houses of Yan and Zhao on Yan's attack on Zhao and its defeat at Hao and Dai, and the houses of Chu, Wei and Han on the death of King Zhao of Qin.

passages.title: Shiji IV: Biographies
passages.zh: 史记（四：列传） 平原君虞卿列传：平原君赵胜者，赵之诸公子也。诸子中胜最贤，喜宾客，宾客盖至者数千人。平原君相赵惠文王及孝成王，三去相，三复位，封於东武城。 平原君家楼临民家。民家有躄者，槃散行汲。平原君美人居楼上，临见，大笑之。明日，躄者至平原君门，请曰：“臣闻君之喜士，士不远千里而至者，以君能贵士而贱妾也。臣不幸有罢癃之病，而君之後宫临而笑臣，臣原得笑臣者头。”平原君笑应曰：“诺。”躄者去，平原君笑曰：“观此竖子，乃欲以一笑之故杀吾美人，不亦甚乎！”终不杀。居岁馀，宾客门下舍人稍稍引去者过半。平原君怪之，曰：“胜所以待诸君者未尝敢失礼，而去者何多也？”门下一人前对曰：“以君之不杀笑躄者，以君为爱色而贱士，士即去耳。”於是平原君乃斩笑躄者美人头，自造门进躄者，因谢焉。其後门下乃复稍稍来。是时齐有孟尝，魏有信陵，楚有春申，故争相倾以待士。 秦之围邯郸，赵使平原君求救，合从於楚，约与食客门下有勇力文武备具者二十人偕。平原君曰：“使文能取胜，则善矣。文不能取胜，则歃血於华屋之下，必得定从而还。士不外索，取於食客门下足矣。”得十九人，馀无可取者，无以满二十人。门下有毛遂者，前，自赞於平原君曰：“遂闻君将合从於楚，约与食客门下二十人偕，不外索。今少一人，原君即以遂备员而行矣。”平原君曰：“先生处胜之门下几年於此矣？”毛遂曰：“三年於此矣。”平原君曰：“夫贤士之处世也，譬若锥之处囊中，其末立见。今先生处胜之门下三年於此矣，左右未有所称诵，胜未有所闻，是先生无所有也。先生不能，先生留。”毛遂曰：“臣乃今日请处囊中耳。使遂蚤得处囊中，乃颖脱而出，非特其末见而已。”平原君竟与毛遂偕。十九人相与目笑之而未废也。 毛遂比至楚，与十九人论议，十九人皆服。平原君与楚合从，言其利害，日出而言之，日中不决。十九人谓毛遂曰：“先生上。”毛遂按剑历阶而上，谓平原君曰：“从之利害，两言而决耳。今日出而言从，日中不决，何也？”楚王谓平原君曰：“客何为者也？”平原君曰：“是胜之舍人也。”楚王叱曰：“胡不下！吾乃与而君言，汝何为者也！”毛遂按剑而前曰：“王之所以叱遂者，以楚国之众也。今十步之内，王不得恃楚国之众也，王之命县於遂手。吾君在前，叱者何也？且遂闻汤以七十里之地王天下，文王以百里之壤而臣诸侯，岂其士卒众多哉，诚能据其势而奋其威。今楚地方五千里，持戟百万，此霸王之资也。以楚之彊，天下弗能当。白起，小竖子耳，率数万之众，兴师以与楚战，一战而举鄢郢，再战而烧夷陵，三战而辱王之先人。此百世之怨而赵之所羞，而王弗知恶焉。合从者为楚，非为赵也。吾君在前，叱者何也？”楚王曰：“唯唯，诚若先生之言，谨奉社稷而以从。”毛遂曰：“从定乎？”楚王曰：“定矣。”毛遂谓楚王之左右曰：“取鸡狗马之血来。”毛遂奉铜槃而跪进之楚王曰：“王当歃血而定从，次者吾君，次者遂。”遂定从於殿上。毛遂左手持槃血而右手招十九人曰：“公相与歃此血於堂下。公等录录，所谓因人成事者也。” 平原君已定从而归，归至於赵，曰：“胜不敢复相士。胜相士多者千人，寡者百数，自以为不失天下之士，今乃於毛先生而失之也。毛先生一至楚，而使赵重於九鼎大吕。毛先生以三寸之舌，强于百万之师。胜不敢复相士。”遂以为上客。 平原君既返赵，楚使春申君将兵赴救赵，魏信陵君亦矫夺晋鄙军往救赵，皆未至。秦急围邯郸，邯郸急，且降，平原君甚患之。邯郸传舍吏子李同说平原君曰：“君不忧赵亡邪？”平原君曰：“赵亡则胜为虏，何为不忧乎？”李同曰：“邯郸之民，炊骨易子而食，可谓急矣，而君之後宫以百数，婢妾被绮縠，馀粱肉，而民褐衣不完，糟糠不厌。民困兵尽，或剡木为矛矢，而君器物锺磬自若。使秦破赵，君安得有此？使赵得全，君何患无有？今君诚能令夫人以下编於士卒之间，分功而作，家之所有尽散以飨士，士方其危苦之时，易德耳。”於是平原君从之，得敢死之士三千人。李同遂与三千人赴秦军，秦军为之卻三十里。亦会楚、魏救至，秦兵遂罢，邯郸复存。李同战死，封其父为李侯。 虞卿欲以信陵君之存邯郸为平原君请封。公孙龙闻之，夜驾见平原君曰：“龙闻虞卿欲以信陵君之存邯郸为君请封，有之乎？”平原君曰：“然。”龙曰：“此甚不可。且王举君而相赵者，非以君之智能为赵国无有也。割东武城而封君者，非以君为有功也，而以国人无勋，乃以君为亲戚故也。君受相印不辞无能，割地不言无功者，亦自以为亲戚故也。今信陵君存邯郸而请封，是亲戚受城而国人计功也。此甚不可。且虞卿操其两权，事成，操右券以责；事不成，以虚名德君。君必勿听也。”平原君遂不听虞卿。 平原君以赵孝成王十五年卒。子孙代，後竟与赵俱亡。 廉颇蔺相如列传：自邯郸围解五年，而燕用栗腹之谋，曰“赵壮者尽於长平，其孤未壮”，举兵击赵。赵使廉颇将，击，大破燕军於鄗，杀栗腹，遂围燕。燕割五城请和，乃听之。赵以尉文封廉颇为信平君，为假相国。 廉颇之免长平归也，失势之时，故客尽去。及复用为将，客又复至。廉颇曰：“客退矣！”客曰：“吁！君何见之晚也？夫天下以市道交，君有势，我则从君，君无势则去，此固其理也，有何怨乎？”居六年，赵使廉颇伐魏之繁阳，拔之。
passages.en: Shiji IV: Biographies Biography of Lord Pingyuan and Yu Qing: Lord Pingyuan, Zhao Sheng, was one of the Princes of Zhao. Among the princes Sheng was the worthiest; he was fond of retainers, and the retainers who came to him numbered some several thousand. Lord Pingyuan was Chancellor to King Huiwen of Zhao and to King Xiaocheng; three times he left the chancellorship and three times he was restored to it. He was enfeoffed at Dongwucheng. A storeyed building of Lord Pingyuan's house overlooked the house of a commoner. In the commoner's house there was a lame man, who hobbled out to draw water. A beauty of Lord Pingyuan's who lived in the upper storey looked down, saw him and laughed loudly at him. The next day the lame man came to Lord Pingyuan's gate and begged: "Your servant has heard that you, my lord, are fond of gentlemen, and that gentlemen do not think a thousand li too far to come to you, because you are able to honour gentlemen and hold women cheap. Your servant has the misfortune to be afflicted with a crooked back, and a woman of your rear palace looked down and laughed at me. I beg to be given the head of the one who laughed at me." Lord Pingyuan laughed and answered: "Agreed." When the lame man had gone, Lord Pingyuan laughed and said: "Look at this fellow: for the sake of a single laugh he wants to kill my beauty. Is that not going too far?" In the end he did not kill her. A year or more passed, and more than half of his retainers and the household retainers under his gate drifted away. Lord Pingyuan thought it strange and said: "In my treatment of you gentlemen I, Sheng, have never dared to fail in courtesy; why then are so many leaving?" One of those under his gate came forward and answered: "Because you did not kill the one who laughed at the lame man, they take you for one who loves beauty and holds gentlemen cheap, and so the gentlemen leave." Thereupon Lord Pingyuan cut off the head of the beauty who had laughed at the lame man, went in person to his door, presented it to the lame man, and apologised to him. After that those under his gate gradually came back. At that time Qi had Mengchang, Wei had Xinling and Chu had Chunshen, and so they competed to outdo one another in receiving gentlemen. When Qin besieged Handan, Zhao sent Lord Pingyuan to seek relief and to join the Vertical Alliance with Chu; he arranged to take with him twenty of the retainers under his gate who had courage and strength and were complete in both civil and martial accomplishments. Lord Pingyuan said: "If the victory can be won by civil means, very good. If it cannot be won by civil means, then we shall smear the blood beneath the splendid hall, and I shall without fail settle the Alliance before I return. Gentlemen are not to be sought outside; to take them from the retainers under my gate will suffice." He found nineteen, and among the rest there was none fit to take, so he had no way to make up the twenty. Among those under his gate was one Mao Sui, who came forward and commended himself to Lord Pingyuan: "Sui has heard that you, my lord, are about to join the Vertical Alliance with Chu and have arranged to take twenty of the retainers under your gate with you, not seeking outside. Now you are one man short; I beg you, my lord, to make up the number with Sui and set out." Lord Pingyuan said: "How many years, sir, have you been under my gate?" Mao Sui said: "Three years now." Lord Pingyuan said: "A worthy gentleman's place in the world is like an awl's place in a bag: its point shows at once. Now you, sir, have been under my gate three years, and those about me have had nothing to say in your praise, nor have I heard anything of you; that means you have nothing in you, sir. You are not able, sir; you will stay." Mao Sui said: "It is only today that your servant asks to be put in the bag. Had Sui been put in the bag earlier, the whole of him would have come through, not merely his point." In the end Lord Pingyuan took Mao Sui with him. The nineteen exchanged glances and smiled at him, but did not yet cast him off. By the time Mao Sui reached Chu he had debated with the nineteen, and all nineteen submitted to him. Lord Pingyuan treated with Chu for the Vertical Alliance, setting out its advantages and disadvantages; he spoke of it from sunrise, and by midday nothing was decided. The nineteen said to Mao Sui: "Go up, sir." Mao Sui, his hand on his sword, mounted the steps and went up, and said to Lord Pingyuan: "The advantages and disadvantages of the Alliance can be decided in two words. Today you have spoken of the Alliance since sunrise and by midday it is not decided; why is that?" The King of Chu said to Lord Pingyuan: "What is this guest?" Lord Pingyuan said: "This is a household retainer of mine." The King of Chu shouted at him: "Why do you not go down! I am speaking with your master; what are you!" Mao Sui, his hand on his sword, stepped forward and said: "Your Majesty shouts at Sui because of the multitude of the state of Chu. But now, within these ten paces, Your Majesty cannot rely on the multitude of Chu: Your Majesty's life hangs in Sui's hand. My master is before you; what is this shouting? Moreover, Sui has heard that Tang with seventy li of land became king of all under Heaven, and King Wen with a hundred li of soil made the Lords his subjects. Was it that their soldiers were many? It was that they were truly able to hold their position and put forth their might. Now Chu's territory is five thousand li square, and it has a million halberd-bearers: that is the stuff of a hegemon king. With Chu's strength nothing under Heaven can withstand it. Bai Qi is a mere stripling, yet at the head of a few tens of thousands he raised an army to fight Chu: in one battle he took Yan and Ying, in a second he burned Yiling, in a third he disgraced Your Majesty's ancestors. That is a grudge for a hundred generations and a thing Zhao is ashamed of on your behalf, yet Your Majesty does not know to hate it. The Alliance is for Chu's sake, not for Zhao's. My master is before you; what is this shouting?" The King of Chu said: "Yes, yes. It is truly as you say, sir: I shall reverently commit the altars of soil and grain to the Alliance." Mao Sui said: "Is the Alliance settled?" The King of Chu said: "It is settled." Mao Sui said to the King of Chu's attendants: "Bring the blood of a cock, a dog and a horse." Mao Sui held up the bronze basin, knelt and offered it to the King of Chu, saying: "Your Majesty should smear the blood and settle the Alliance; next my master, next Sui." So the Alliance was settled in the upper hall. Mao Sui, holding the basin of blood in his left hand, beckoned with his right to the nineteen and said: "You gentlemen shall smear this blood together below the hall. You, sirs, are mere followers, what is called accomplishing things through others." When Lord Pingyuan had settled the Alliance and returned, on reaching Zhao he said: "Sheng will never again dare to judge gentlemen. Of the gentlemen Sheng has judged, at most a thousand, at least some hundreds, I thought I had let no gentleman of the world slip past me; and now in Master Mao I let one slip. Master Mao went once to Chu and made Zhao weightier than the Nine Tripods and the Great Lü. With a tongue three inches long Master Mao was stronger than an army of a million. Sheng will never again dare to judge gentlemen." And he made him a guest of the first rank. When Lord Pingyuan had returned to Zhao, Chu sent Lord Chunshen at the head of troops to hasten to Zhao's relief, and Lord Xinling of Wei too, feigning a command, seized Jin Bi's army and went to Zhao's relief; but neither had yet arrived. Qin pressed the siege of Handan hard; Handan was in straits and about to surrender, and Lord Pingyuan was greatly troubled by it. Li Tong, son of an officer of the post-house of Handan, advised Lord Pingyuan: "Are you not anxious, my lord, that Zhao will perish?" Lord Pingyuan said: "If Zhao perishes, Sheng will be a captive; how could I not be anxious?" Li Tong said: "The people of Handan cook bones for fuel and exchange their children to eat: that may be called straits indeed. Yet your rear palace numbers its women by the hundred, your maids and concubines are clothed in figured silk and gauze and have fine grain and meat to spare, while the people's coarse clothes are in tatters and they cannot get their fill of husks and chaff. The people are exhausted and the weapons used up, some sharpening wood into spears and arrows, while your vessels, your bells and chimes, remain as they were. If Qin breaks Zhao, how will you keep these, my lord? If Zhao comes through whole, what fear have you of lacking them? Now if you, my lord, could truly have your ladies and those below them enrolled among the soldiers, sharing the work according to their tasks, and could disperse all that your house holds to feast the gentlemen: gentlemen in their hour of danger and hardship are easily won by kindness." Thereupon Lord Pingyuan followed his advice and obtained three thousand gentlemen ready to die. Li Tong then went with the three thousand against the Qin army, and the Qin army fell back thirty li before them. It happened too that the relief from Chu and Wei arrived; the Qin troops then withdrew, and Handan survived. Li Tong died in the fighting, and his father was enfeoffed as Marquis of Li. Yu Qing wished to ask a fief for Lord Pingyuan on the ground that Lord Xinling had saved Handan. When Gongsun Long heard of it, he drove by night to see Lord Pingyuan and said: "Long has heard that Yu Qing wishes to ask a fief for you, my lord, on the ground that Lord Xinling saved Handan. Is it so?" Lord Pingyuan said: "It is." Long said: "This is quite wrong. The King raised you to be Chancellor of Zhao not because there was no one in the state of Zhao with your wisdom and ability; he cut off Dongwucheng and enfeoffed you not because you had merit, nor because the men of the state had no achievements, but because you are his kin. When you accepted the Chancellor's seal you did not decline it as beyond your ability, and when land was cut off for you you did not say you had no merit, because you too held it to be on account of your kinship. Now, when Lord Xinling has saved Handan, to ask for a fief would be for a kinsman to receive a Fortress while the men of the state reckon up merit. This is quite wrong. Besides, Yu Qing holds both ends: if the affair succeeds, he holds the right-hand tally and claims his due; if it fails, he puts you in his debt for the empty name of it. You must not listen to him." So Lord Pingyuan did not listen to Yu Qing. Lord Pingyuan died in the fifteenth year of King Xiaocheng of Zhao. His sons and grandsons succeeded him, and in the end they perished together with Zhao. Biography of Lian Po and Lin Xiangru: Five years after the siege of Handan was raised, Yan adopted Li Fu's plan — "those of Zhao in their prime were all used up at Changping, and their orphans are not yet grown" — and raised troops to strike at Zhao. Zhao sent Lian Po in command; he struck and heavily defeated the Yan army at Hao, killed Li Fu, and went on to besiege Yan. Yan ceded five Fortresses and sued for peace, and this was granted. Zhao enfeoffed Lian Po with Weiwen as Lord Xinping and made him Acting Chancellor of State. When Lian Po had been dismissed at Changping and returned home, in the time when he had lost his position, his old retainers all left. When he was again employed as general, the retainers came back again. Lian Po said: "Retainers, withdraw!" A retainer said: "Ah! How late you are in seeing it, my lord! All under Heaven make their friendships as in the market: when you have position I follow you, and when you have none I leave. That is the plain principle of it; what is there to resent?" After six years, Zhao sent Lian Po to attack Wei's Fanyang, and he took it.
passages.no: 槃散: the Jijie: also written 跚; the Suoyin: 散 is pronounced as 跚; the Zhengyi: 躄 means lame. 罢癃: the Suoyin: an ailment of the back, the waist bent and the back humped; Xu Guang: 癃 is an illness. 待: Xu Guang: one text reads 得, "winning". 颖脱而出: the Suoyin cites Zheng Xuan, 颖 is the ring; the whole awl would come through the bag, down to the ring of its handle. The Suoyin cites Zheng Xuan: they all looked at him and smiled lightly, but could not yet discard him. 恶: the Zhengyi gives the pronunciation 烏故反, wu in the falling tone, "to hate". The Suoyin: the victims of a covenant differ by rank, the Son of Heaven using an ox and a horse, the Lords a dog and a boar, Grand Masters and below a cock; here the blood of the covenant is named in general, hence "the blood of a cock, a dog and a horse". The Suoyin: by the Rites of Zhou a pearl basin would be used. 录录: the Jijie and the Suoyin give the pronunciation lu; the Suoyin cites the Shuowen, "the look of one who follows along". 大吕: the Zhengyi: the great bell of the Zhou ancestral temple; the Suoyin: the Nine Tripods and the Great Lü are the treasured vessels of the state, so that Zhao was made weighty in the eyes of the world. 易德: the Zhengyi: gentlemen in their hour of danger and hardship easily feel gratitude. Xu Guang: one text reads 是亲戚受城而以国许人, "for a kinsman to receive a Fortress and to promise the state to others". 右券: the Suoyin: if Yu Qing's proposal of a fief succeeds, he holds the right-hand half of the tally with which to claim the return of his favour. 251 BC. The Suoyin here says that the Table of the Six States and the Hereditary House both give the fourteenth year, unlike this; the Table as it stands gives the fifteenth, and the Suoyin on the Hereditary House cites it so. The Jijie, Xu Guang: 尉文 is the name of a town; the Suoyin: 信平 is a title; the Hanshu's table has a Marquis Jie of Weiwen 尉文节侯, placed in Nan Commandery, so probably 尉 is an office and 文 a name, and the town that Wen had held in fief was given anew to Po, who was then styled Lord Xinping. 遂: Mao Sui naming himself; Lord Pingyuan calls him Master Mao 毛先生 below. 龙: Gongsun Long naming himself. The Biographies for this year: the Biography of Lord Pingyuan and Yu Qing, excerpted from the beginning to Lord Pingyuan's death in this year, and the lines of the Biography of Lian Po and Lin Xiangru on the defeat of Yan and Lian Po's enfeoffment.

passages.title: Shiji V: Biographies
passages.zh: 史记（五：列传） 吕不韦列传：秦昭王五十六年，薨，太子安国君立为王，华阳夫人为王后，子楚为太子。赵亦奉子楚夫人及子政归秦。
passages.en: Shiji V: Biographies Biography of Lü Buwei: In the fifty-sixth year of King Zhao of Qin he died; the Heir Apparent, Lord Anguo, was set up as king, Lady Huayang became Queen, and Zichu became Heir Apparent. Zhao for its part escorted Zichu's wife and his son Zheng back to Qin.
passages.no: The fifty-sixth year of King Zhaoxiang of Qin, 251 BC; the subject of 薨, "died", is the king. 奉: conveyed with due honour. The lines of the Biography of Lü Buwei on the death of King Zhao of Qin and the return of Zichu's wife and son from Zhao.

passages.title: Ivar the Boneless' commentary and analysis I
passages.zh: 无骨论点补充（以及辨析）一 赵军杀栗腹，虏卿秦，燕昌国君乐间(乐毅之子)奔赵。 赵封廉颇为信平君、守相。 辨析： 乐间，今本《史記·趙世家》作樂閒（簡體：乐闲），宋本《史記·趙世家》有作樂間，有作樂閒，不詳。又，前文有燕昌國君樂閒，三種宋刻本皆為閒。故，閒的可能性更大。
passages.en: Ivar the Boneless' commentary and analysis I The Zhao army killed Li Fu and captured Qing Qin; Yan's Lord Changguo, Yue Jian (the son of Yue Yi), fled to Zhao. Zhao enfeoffed Lian Po as Lord Xinping and made him Acting Chancellor. Analysis: 乐间: the current text of the Shiji, Hereditary House of Zhao, writes 樂閒 (simplified 乐闲); the Song editions of the Hereditary House of Zhao write now 樂間, now 樂閒, and it cannot be settled. Further, the earlier passage has 燕昌國君樂閒 for Yan's Lord Changguo, and all three Song block-print editions there have 閒. Hence 閒 is the more likely.
passages.no: Ivar the Boneless' commentary on the year: Zhao's victory over Yan and Lian Po's enfeoffment, with an analysis of the spelling of Yue Jian's name in the editions of the Shiji.

passages.title: Collected Qin Slips I: the Shuihudi bamboo slips
passages.zh: 《秦简牍合集》（一）睡虎地竹简 葉書：五十六年，後九月，昭死。正月，遬產。
passages.en: Collected Qin Slips I: the Shuihudi bamboo slips Chronicle: In the fifty-sixth year, in the intercalary month after September, Zhao died. In January, Su was born.
passages.no: The fifty-sixth year of King Zhaoxiang of Qin, 251 BC. 後九月, "the later ninth month": the intercalary month, which the Qin calendar added at the end of the year after the ninth month. The Qin year began with the tenth month, so the January of the next notice falls earlier in the same year. 昭: King Zhaoxiang of Qin; the Basic Annals put his death in the autumn of the year. The entry for 251 BC in the Chronicle of the Shuihudi slips: the death of King Zhaoxiang and the birth of Su.

passages.title: Shiji I: Basic Annals
passages.zh: 史记（一：本纪） 秦本纪：孝文王元年，赦罪人，修先王功臣，褒厚亲戚，弛苑囿。孝文王除丧，十月己亥即位，三日辛丑卒，子庄襄王立。
passages.en: Shiji I: Basic Annals Basic Annals of Qin: In the first year of King Xiaowen, he pardoned offenders, honoured the meritorious servants of the former kings, bestowed generous favour on his kinsmen, and opened the parks and preserves. When King Xiaowen had put off mourning, he came to the throne in October, on the day Jihai; on the third day, Xinchou, he died, and his son King Zhuangxiang was set up.
passages.no: The first and only year of King Xiaowen of Qin, 250 BC. 修先王功臣: 修 here is to attend to, to treat well. 弛苑囿: 弛, to relax; the enclosed parks and preserves of the king were opened. 十月: the Qin year began with the tenth month, so this October stands at the head of the year; the month began in what is, by the Julian reckoning, late October 251 BC. 三日: the third day counting from the accession day, Jihai, Gengzi, Xinchou. The Basic Annals for 250 BC: the entry of the Basic Annals of Qin under the first year of King Xiaowen, his acts on accession, his three-day reign and his death.

passages.title: Shiji III: Hereditary Houses
passages.zh: 史记（三：世家） 赵世家：十六年，廉颇围燕。以乐乘为武襄君。
passages.en: Shiji III: Hereditary Houses Hereditary House of Zhao: In the sixteenth year, Lian Po besieged Yan. Yue Cheng was made Lord Wuxiang.
passages.no: The sixteenth year of King Xiaocheng of Zhao, 250 BC. 武襄: the Zhengyi: 襄 means to raise up, to be above, the title saying that Yue Cheng's merit was the highest. The entry of the Hereditary House of Zhao for this year: Lian Po's siege of Yan and Yue Cheng's title.

When he was again employed as general, the retainers came back again. Lian Po said: "Retainers, withdraw!" A retainer said: "Ah! How late you are in seeing it, my lord! All under Heaven make their friendships as in the market: when you have position I follow you, and when you have none I leave. That is the plain principle of it; what is there to resent?" After six years, Zhao sent Lian Po to attack Wei's Fanyang, and he took it.
passages.no: The Jijie, Xu Guang: 尉文 is the name of a town; the Suoyin: 信平 is a title; the Hanshu's table has a Marquis Jie of Weiwen 尉文节侯, placed in Nan Commandery, so probably 尉 is an office and 文 a name, and the town that Wen had held in fief was given anew to Po, who was then styled Lord Xinping. The lines of the Biography of Lian Po and Lin Xiangru on the defeat of Yan and Lian Po's enfeoffment, given under this year as well, in which the Hereditary House of Zhao places the siege of Yan.

passages.title: Shiji V: Biographies
passages.zh: 史记（五：列传） 吕不韦列传： 秦王立一年，薨，谥为孝文王。太子子楚代立，是为庄襄王。庄襄王所母华阳后为华阳太后，真母夏姬尊以为夏太后。
passages.en: Shiji V: Biographies Biography of Lü Buwei: The King of Qin had been on the throne one year when he died; his posthumous title was Xiaowen. The Heir Apparent, Zichu, succeeded him; this was King Zhuangxiang. The one King Zhuangxiang had as his mother, Queen Huayang, became Queen Dowager Huayang, and his real mother, Lady Xia, was honoured as Queen Dowager Xia.
passages.no: 所母: the mother by adoption, Queen Huayang, as against the 真母, the real mother; the Suoyin: Liu's text reads 所生母, with 生 an intrusive character, and the editions it checked have no 生. The lines of the Biography of Lü Buwei on the death of King Xiaowen, the accession of King Zhuangxiang and the two Queens Dowager.

passages.title: Ivar the Boneless' commentary and analysis I
passages.zh: 无骨论点补充（以及辨析）一 赵将李牧大破匈奴十馀万骑，灭襜褴，破东胡，降林胡，单于奔走。 辨析：《史記·廉頗藺相如列傳》： 李牧者，赵之北边良将也。常居代雁门，备匈奴。以便宜置吏，市租皆输入莫府，为士卒费。日击数牛飨士，习射骑，谨烽火，多间谍，厚遇战士。为约曰：“匈奴即入盗，急入收保，有敢捕虏者斩。”匈奴每入，烽火谨，辄入收保，不敢战。如是数岁，亦不亡失。然匈奴以李牧为怯，虽赵边兵亦以为吾将怯。赵王让李牧，李牧如故。赵王怒，召之，使他人代将。 岁馀，匈奴每来，出战。出战，数不利，失亡多，边不得田畜。复请李牧。牧杜门不出，固称疾。赵王乃复强起使将兵。牧曰：“王必用臣，臣如前，乃敢奉令。”王许之。 李牧至，如故约。匈奴数岁无所得。终以为怯。边士日得赏赐而不用，皆原一战。於是乃具选车得千三百乘，选骑得万三千匹，百金之士五万人，彀者十万人，悉勒习战。大纵畜牧，人民满野。匈奴小入，详北不胜，以数千人委之。单于闻之，大率众来入。李牧多为奇陈，张左右翼击之，大破杀匈奴十馀万骑。灭襜褴，破东胡，降林胡，单于奔走。其後十馀岁，匈奴不敢近赵边城。 《史記·趙世家》載李牧為將是趙悼襄王二年（前243），李牧與匈奴的戰事年代不詳。又，《史記·匈奴列傳》：其后赵将李牧时，匈奴不敢入赵边。 李牧與匈奴的戰事或在趙悼襄王二年（前243）後。“其後十馀岁”或指趙悼襄王至秦滅趙的十餘年間。
passages.en: Ivar the Boneless' commentary and analysis I The Zhao general Li Mu heavily defeated more than a hundred thousand Xiongnu horsemen, destroyed the Danlan, broke the Donghu, brought the Linhu to submission, and the Chanyu fled. Analysis: Shiji, Biography of Lian Po and Lin Xiangru: Li Mu was a fine general of Zhao's northern frontier. He was regularly stationed at Yanmen in Dai, on guard against the Xiongnu. He appointed officers at his own discretion, and the market taxes were all paid into his headquarters for the soldiers' expenses. Every day he slaughtered several oxen to feast his men; he drilled them in archery and riding, kept careful watch on the beacon fires, used many spies, and treated the fighting men generously. He laid down a rule: "When the Xiongnu come in to raid, withdraw at once into the strongholds; anyone who dares to take captives will be beheaded." Whenever the Xiongnu came in, the beacons gave careful warning and the men withdrew at once into the strongholds and did not dare to fight. So it went for several years, and nothing was lost either. But the Xiongnu took Li Mu for a coward, and even the Zhao frontier troops thought their general a coward. The King of Zhao reproved Li Mu, but Li Mu went on as before. The King of Zhao was angry, recalled him, and had another man take over the command. After a year or more, whenever the Xiongnu came, the army went out to fight. Going out to fight, it was repeatedly worsted, the losses were many, and on the frontier there was no farming or herding. The king again asked for Li Mu. Mu shut his gate and would not come out, insisting that he was ill. The King of Zhao then pressed him again to rise and sent him to command the troops. Mu said: "If Your Majesty must employ your servant, your servant will dare to accept the command only if he may do as before." The king consented. Li Mu arrived and kept to the old rule. For several years the Xiongnu got nothing, and to the end they took him for a coward. The frontier soldiers received rewards every day and were never used, and all of them wished for a single battle. Thereupon he fitted out picked chariots, and got thirteen hundred; picked horsemen, and got thirteen thousand; soldiers of the hundred jin of gold, fifty thousand; and bowmen, a hundred thousand; and he drilled them all for battle. He let the herds out to graze far and wide, and the people filled the open country. The Xiongnu came in with a small force; he feigned defeat and abandoned several thousand men to them. When the Chanyu heard of it, he came in at the head of a great host. Li Mu set many unexpected formations, spread out his left and right wings and struck, and heavily defeated and killed more than a hundred thousand Xiongnu horsemen. He destroyed the Danlan, broke the Donghu, brought the Linhu to submission, and the Chanyu fled. For more than ten years after that the Xiongnu did not dare to come near the frontier Fortresses of Zhao. The Shiji, Hereditary House of Zhao, records Li Mu as general in the second year of King Daoxiang of Zhao (243 BC); the date of Li Mu's war with the Xiongnu is not known. Further, the Shiji, Account of the Xiongnu: "Later, in the time of the Zhao general Li Mu, the Xiongnu did not dare to enter the Zhao frontier." Li Mu's war with the Xiongnu was perhaps after the second year of King Daoxiang of Zhao (243 BC). "For more than ten years after that" perhaps means the ten-odd years from King Daoxiang to Qin's destruction of Zhao.
passages.no: 代雁门: the Zhengyi: Yanmen County lies in the land of Dai, hence "Dai Yanmen". 莫府: the Jijie cites Ru Chun, a general on campaign has no fixed seat and governs wherever he is, hence 莫府, 莫 meaning great; the Suoyin cites Cui Hao, the commander's office was set up under tents (幕), so 莫 should be 幕, a graphic error. The King of Zhao is not named in the passage. 畜: the Zhengyi gives the pronunciation 许六反, xu, to rear animals. 百金之士: the Jijie cites the Guanzi, "those able to break the enemy and capture a general are rewarded with a hundred jin". 彀者: the Suoyin: 彀 means able to shoot. 委之: the Suoyin: 委 means to abandon them, letting the enemy kill and plunder at will. 襜褴: the Jijie gives the pronunciations 都甘反 and 路談反, dan lan; Xu Guang: one text reads 临; Ru Chun: the name of a Hu people, north of Dai. Ivar the Boneless' commentary on the year: Li Mu's victory over the Xiongnu, with the passage of the Biography of Lian Po and Lin Xiangru on which it rests and an analysis of its date.

passages.title: Collected Qin Slips I: the Shuihudi bamboo slips
passages.zh: 《秦简牍合集》（一）睡虎地竹简 葉書：孝文王元年，立即死。
passages.en: Collected Qin Slips I: the Shuihudi bamboo slips Chronicle: First year of King Xiaowen; set up, and died at once.
passages.no: The first year of King Xiaowen of Qin, 250 BC. 立即死: the subject, King Xiaowen, is not expressed; the Basic Annals of Qin have him die on the third day after his accession. The entry for 250 BC in the Chronicle of the Shuihudi slips: the accession and immediate death of King Xiaowen.

passages.title: Shiji I: Basic Annals
passages.zh: 史记（一：本纪） 周本纪：后七岁，秦庄襄王灭东周。东西周皆入于秦，周既不祀。 秦本纪：庄襄王元年，大赦罪人，修先王功臣，施德厚骨肉而布惠于民。东周君与诸侯谋秦，秦使相国吕不韦诛之，尽入其国。秦不绝其祀，以阳人地赐周君，奉其祭祀。使蒙骜伐韩，韩献成皋、巩。秦界至大梁，初置三川郡。
passages.en: Shiji I: Basic Annals Basic Annals of Zhou: Seven years later, King Zhuangxiang of Qin destroyed Eastern Zhou. Eastern and Western Zhou both passed into Qin's hands, and Zhou's sacrifices ended altogether. Basic Annals of Qin: In the first year of King Zhuangxiang, he granted a great pardon to offenders, honoured the meritorious servants of the former kings, showed favour and generosity to his kin, and spread his bounty among the people. The Lord of Eastern Zhou plotted against Qin with the Lords; Qin sent the Chancellor of State Lü Buwei to punish him and took in the whole of his state. Qin did not cut off his sacrifices: it granted the Lord of Zhou the land of Yangren so that he might keep up his sacrifices. It sent Meng Ao to attack Han, and Han presented Chenggao and Gong. Qin's border reached to Daliang, and for the first time Sanchuan Commandery was established.
passages.no: 後七歲: seven years on from the Annals' previous entry, the end of Western Zhou in 256 BC. Xu Guang: when Zhou was about to perish it had seven Counties in all, Henan, Luoyang, Gucheng, Pingyin, Yanshi, Gong and Goushi. 既: the Suoyin: wholly, as of an eclipse that is total; the line of Zhou was extinguished and there was no one to keep its sacrifices. The Jijie cites Huangfu Mi: Zhou had thirty-seven kings and eight hundred and sixty-seven years in all. The first year of King Zhuangxiang of Qin, 249 BC. The Basic Annals for 249 BC: the Basic Annals of Zhou on the end of Eastern Zhou, and the Basic Annals of Qin under the first year of King Zhuangxiang, with Lü Buwei's suppression of Eastern Zhou, Meng Ao's campaign against Han and the founding of Sanchuan Commandery.

passages.title: Shiji II: Tables
passages.zh: 史记（二：表） 秦：蒙驚取成皋、榮陽，初置三川郡。呂不韋相，取東周。 韓：秦拔我成皋、榮陽。 楚：楚滅魯，頃公遷卞，為家人，絕祀。
passages.en: Shiji II: Tables Qin: Meng Ao took Chenggao and Xingyang; Sanchuan Commandery was established for the first time. Lü Buwei became Chancellor. Took Eastern Zhou. Han: Qin took our Chenggao and Xingyang. Chu: Chu destroyed Lu; Duke Qing was moved to Bian, became a commoner, and the sacrifices were cut off.
passages.no: 蒙驚: the three-commentary edition reads 蒙驁, Meng Ao, as the Basic Annals above. 榮陽: the three-commentary edition reads 滎陽, Xingyang. 我: the Table speaks from the standpoint of the state whose column it is, so "our Chenggao and Xingyang" are Han's. 家人: a private person, one without rank or fief. The row of the Table of the Six States for this year: the entries for Qin, Han and Chu.

passages.title: Shiji III: Hereditary Houses
passages.zh: 史记（三：世家） 鲁周公世家：二十四年，楚考烈王伐灭鲁。顷公亡，迁于下邑，为家人，鲁绝祀。顷公卒于柯。 鲁起周公至顷公，凡三十四世。 燕召公世家：六年，秦灭东周，置三川郡。 赵世家：十七年，假相大将武襄君攻燕，围其国。 韩世家：二十四年，秦拔我城皋、荥阳。 田敬仲完世家：十六年，秦灭周。君王后卒。
passages.en: Shiji III: Hereditary Houses Hereditary House of the Duke of Zhou of Lu: In the twenty-fourth year, King Kaolie of Chu attacked and destroyed Lu. Duke Qing fled and was moved to an outlying settlement; he became a commoner, and Lu's sacrifices were cut off. Duke Qing died at Ke. From the Duke of Zhou to Duke Qing, Lu had thirty-four generations in all. Hereditary House of Duke Shao of Yan: In the sixth year, Qin destroyed Eastern Zhou and established Sanchuan Commandery. Hereditary House of Zhao: In the seventeenth year, the Acting Chancellor and great general Lord Wuxiang attacked Yan and besieged its capital. Hereditary House of Han: In the twenty-fourth year, Qin took our Chenggao and Xingyang. Hereditary House of Tian Jingzhong Wan: In the sixteenth year, Qin destroyed Zhou. Queen Jun died.
passages.no: The twenty-fourth year of Duke Qing of Lu, 249 BC. 下邑: the Suoyin: a small settlement away from the capital; Xu Guang: 下 is written 卞 in one text, and the Suoyin notes that Lu did have a settlement called Bian, which is the cause of the confusion. The Table gives Bian. 柯: the Suoyin cites the Chunqiu, "Qi attacked Lu at Ke and made a covenant", and Du Yu, Ke is a Qi settlement, now Dong'e in Jibei. The Jijie cites Huangfu Mi on Duke Qing's reign, from a wuzi year to a xinhai year. The sixth year of King Xi of Yan, 249 BC. The seventeenth year of King Xiaocheng of Zhao, 249 BC; 国 is the capital of Yan. The twenty-fourth year of King Huanhui of Han, 249 BC; 我, "our", speaks from Han's standpoint. 城皋: written 成皋 in the Basic Annals and the Table. The sixteenth year of King Jian of Qi, 249 BC. The entries of the Hereditary Houses for this year: the house of Lu on its extinction by Chu, and the houses of Yan, Zhao, Han and Qi.

passages.title: Shiji IV: Biographies
passages.zh: 史记（四：列传） 春申君列传：春申君相十四年，秦庄襄王立，以吕不韦为相，封为文信侯。取东周。
passages.en: Shiji IV: Biographies Biography of Lord Chunshen: In the fourteenth year of Lord Chunshen's chancellorship, King Zhuangxiang of Qin came to the throne; he made Lü Buwei Chancellor and enfeoffed him as Marquis Wenxin. Took Eastern Zhou.
passages.no: The fourteenth year of Lord Chunshen as Chancellor of Chu, 249 BC. The subject, Qin, is not expressed. The lines of the Biography of Lord Chunshen on the accession of King Zhuangxiang of Qin, Lü Buwei's chancellorship and the taking of Eastern Zhou.

passages.title: Shiji V: Biographies
passages.zh: 史记（五：列传） 吕不韦列传：庄襄王元年，以吕不韦为丞相，封为文信侯，食河南雒阳十万户。 蒙恬列传：蒙恬者，其先齐人也。恬大父蒙骜，自齐事秦昭王，官至上卿。秦庄襄王元年，蒙骜为秦将，伐韩，取成皋、荥阳，作置三川郡。
passages.en: Shiji V: Biographies Biography of Lü Buwei: In the first year of King Zhuangxiang, he made Lü Buwei Chancellor, enfeoffed him as Marquis Wenxin, and gave him Luoyang in Henan, a hundred thousand households, as his fief. Biography of Meng Tian: Meng Tian's forebears were men of Qi. Tian's grandfather Meng Ao came from Qi to serve King Zhao of Qin, and rose in office to Senior Minister. In the first year of King Zhuangxiang of Qin, Meng Ao was a general of Qin; he attacked Han, took Chenggao and Xingyang, and set up Sanchuan Commandery.
passages.no: The first year of King Zhuangxiang of Qin, 249 BC. 丞相: the Suoyin notes that the text goes on to say "honoured as Chancellor of State" (相国), and cites the Table of Officials of the Hanshu: both were Qin offices, with gold seal and purple ribbon, charged with assisting the Son of Heaven in the conduct of all affairs; Qin set up a Left and a Right, Gaodi one, later renamed Chancellor of State. 食河南雒阳: 食, to draw the revenue of. The Suoyin: the Zhanguoce has "fed on twelve Counties of Lantian"; the Basic Annals of Qin have Sanchuan Commandery founded in this year, and by the Treatise on Geography Gaozu renamed it Henan, so the Shiji, written later, calls Qin's commandery by its Han name. 骜: the Suoyin gives the pronunciation as that of 敖, ao, and Zou's as 五到反. The lines of the Biography of Lü Buwei on his chancellorship and fief, and of the Biography of Meng Tian on his grandfather Meng Ao's campaign against Han.

passages.title: Ivar the Boneless' commentary and analysis I
passages.zh: 无骨论点补充（以及辨析）一 春平侯担任赵相邦。 辨析：我國曾出土多件春平侯鈹，其中十件銘文刻“十七年，相邦春平侯”。據學者推斷，“十七年”是已知最早的年份，但春平侯何時開始擔任相邦，史書未載，且，趙國相邦應不止一人。
passages.en: Ivar the Boneless' commentary and analysis I Marquis Chunping served as Chancellor of State of Zhao. Analysis: A number of pi blades of Marquis Chunping have been excavated in China, ten of them inscribed "seventeenth year, Chancellor of State Marquis Chunping". Scholars infer that the "seventeenth year" is the earliest year known, but when Marquis Chunping began to serve as Chancellor of State the histories do not record; and moreover Zhao's Chancellors of State were presumably more than one.
passages.no: 十七年: taken as the seventeenth year of King Xiaocheng of Zhao, 249 BC, which is why the notice stands under this year. Ivar the Boneless' commentary on the year: Marquis Chunping as Chancellor of State of Zhao, from the inscribed blades of the seventeenth year.

passages.title: Other ancient works (histories)
passages.zh: 其他古籍（史類） 辨析：楚並瑯琊，遷越王親於吳。 越王勾践灭吴称霸是公元前473年，称霸224年越国灭亡，那就是-473+224=公元前249年 《越绝书·越绝外传记地传》: 越王夫镡以上至无余，久远，世不可纪也。夫镡子允常。允常子勾践，大霸称王，徙琅琊，都也。勾践子与夷，时霸。与夷子子翁，时霸。子翁子不扬，时霸。不扬子无彊，时霸，伐楚，威王灭无彊。无彊子之侯，窃自立为君长。之侯子尊，时君长。尊子亲，失众，楚伐之，走南山。亲以上至勾践，凡八君，都琅琊二百二十四岁。无彊以上霸，称王。之侯以下微弱，称君长。 《吴越春秋》（勾践伐吴外传第十） 二十七年冬，勾践寝疾将卒，谓太子兴夷曰：“吾自禹之后，承元常之德，蒙天灵之祐，神祗之福，从穷越之地籍，楚之前锋，以摧吴王之干戈。跨江涉淮，从晋齐之地，功德巍巍。自致于斯，其可不诫乎？夫霸者之后，难以久立，其慎之哉！”遂卒。 兴夷即位一年卒，子翁；翁卒，子不扬；不扬卒，子无强；强卒，子玉；玉卒，子尊；尊卒，子亲。自勾践至于亲，其历八主，皆称霸，积年二百二十四年，亲众皆失，而去琅邪，徙于吴矣。 自黄帝至少康十世，自禹受禅至少康即位六世，为一百四十四年，少康去颛顼即位，四百二十四年。 黄帝→昌意→颛顼→鲧→禹→启→太康→仲庐→相→少康→无余→无壬（去无余十世）→无曎→夫谭→元常→勾践→兴夷→不寿→不扬→无强→鲁穆柳有幽公为名，王侯自称为君→尊→亲，失琅邪，为楚所灭。 勾践至王亲，历八主，格霸二百二十四年。从无余越国始封，至余善返越国空灭，凡一千九百二十二年。 《续汉书·郡国志四》，刘昭在“吴郡安县”一条下注道: 《越绝》曰，有西岑冢，越王孙开所立，以备春申君，使其子守之，子死遂葬城中。 春申君公元前248年被封于江东(《史记·春申君列传》。由此可知，在公元前三世纪半，江浙地区还存在不服从楚国的越势力。 两位专家告诉记者，连云港锦屏山九龙口古城址，考古界称其为尾矿坝遗址，此前未曾有人将其与越王迁都之地联系在一起。他们通过实地调查发现，遗址是一处周长约十里的古代城址。其城三面环山，东面朝大海。城中已被锦屏山左的磷矿废矿砂所填平，形成方圆十余里、深约20余米的积沙。今露出城中部的当时一高台地尚存，南北长300米，东西宽150米左右。考古学家在此台地表采集到了大量越国风格的陶片残器，经检测均为春秋晚期、战国早期的印纹硬陶。由此证实这些遗物当属越国。 随后，专家又在杜佑的《唐·通典》中找到了锦屏山又叫琅琊山的依据。根据史料记载，锦屏山在秦朝建立之前称朐山，又叫琅琊山。秦始皇时期，立为朐县，秦始皇35年（公元前212年）立石为秦东门。秦始皇28年，秦始皇又在山东筑起琅琊台与琅琊邑相呼应。张志立、彭云认为，由于地名的变迁，琅琊山之名渐渐淡出，许多人由此把越王勾践迁都连云港琅琊山的地点误当作了山东青岛地区胶南市的琅琊山。
passages.en: Other ancient works (histories) Analysis: Chu annexed Langya and moved King Qin of Yue to Wu. King Goujian of Yue destroyed Wu and became hegemon in 473 BC; the state of Yue perished after 224 years of hegemony, which gives −473 + 224 = 249 BC Yuejueshu, Outer Tradition, Record of the Lands: From King Futan of Yue back to Wuyu is remote and far off, and the generations cannot be recorded. Futan's son was Yunchang. Yunchang's son was Goujian, who was a great hegemon and styled himself king; he moved to Langya and made it his capital. Goujian's son Yuyi was hegemon in his time. Yuyi's son Ziweng was hegemon in his time. Ziweng's son Buyang was hegemon in his time. Buyang's son Wujiang was hegemon in his time; he attacked Chu, and King Wei destroyed Wujiang. Wujiang's son Zhihou set himself up without warrant as chieftain. Zhihou's son Zun was chieftain in his time. Zun's son Qin lost his people; Chu attacked him and he fled to the southern hills. From Qin back to Goujian, eight lords in all, had their capital at Langya for two hundred and twenty-four years. From Wujiang upward they were hegemons and styled themselves king; from Zhihou downward they were weak and were styled chieftains. Wu Yue Chunqiu (Outer Tradition of Goujian's Attack on Wu, chapter ten) In the winter of the twenty-seventh year, Goujian lay ill and was about to die, and said to the Heir Apparent Xingyi: "I, descended from Yu, inheriting the virtue of Yuanchang, blessed by the protection of Heaven's spirits and the favour of the gods, from the land of poor and remote Yue, with Chu as my vanguard, broke the shields and spears of the King of Wu. I crossed the Jiang and forded the Huai, passed through the lands of Jin and Qi, and my merit and virtue stood towering. Having brought myself to this, can one fail to take warning? The heirs of a hegemon find it hard to stand for long; be careful of it!" Then he died. Xingyi came to the throne and died after one year; his son was Weng. Weng died; his son was Buyang. Buyang died; his son was Wuqiang. Qiang died; his son was Yu. Yu died; his son was Zun. Zun died; his son was Qin. From Goujian down to Qin there were eight rulers, all styled hegemon, over two hundred and twenty-four years in all; Qin lost all his people, left Langya and moved to Wu. From the Yellow Emperor to Shaokang were ten generations; from Yu's receiving the abdication to Shaokang's accession were six generations, one hundred and forty-four years; from Shaokang back to Zhuanxu's accession, four hundred and twenty-four years. Yellow Emperor → Changyi → Zhuanxu → Gun → Yu → Qi → Taikang → Zhonglu → Xiang → Shaokang → Wuyu → Wuren (ten generations from Wuyu) → Wuyi → Futan → Yuanchang → Goujian → Xingyi → Bushou → Buyang → Wuqiang → Lu Mu Liu, who had Duke You as his name; kings and marquises styled themselves lords → Zun → Qin, who lost Langya and was destroyed by Chu. From Goujian to King Qin, eight rulers, hegemons for two hundred and twenty-four years. From Wuyu's first enfeoffment in Yue to Yushan's return and the emptying and extinction of the state of Yue, one thousand nine hundred and twenty-two years in all. In the Xu Hanshu, Treatise on Commanderies and Kingdoms IV, Liu Zhao notes under the entry "An County, Wu Commandery": The Yuejue says: there is the Xicen tomb, set up by Kai, grandson of the King of Yue, to guard against Lord Chunshen; he had his son hold it, and when the son died he was buried within the Fortress. Lord Chunshen was enfeoffed in Jiangdong in 248 BC (Shiji, Biography of Lord Chunshen). From this it can be known that in the middle of the third century BC there were still Yue forces in the Jiangsu–Zhejiang region that did not submit to Chu. The two experts told the reporter that the ancient walled site at Jiulongkou on Jinpingshan, Lianyungang, which archaeologists call the tailings-dam site, had never before been connected with the place to which the King of Yue moved his capital. By survey on the ground they found the site to be an ancient walled city about ten li in circumference. The city is ringed by hills on three sides and faces the sea on the east. Its interior has been filled by the waste sand of the phosphate mine to the left of Jinpingshan, forming an accumulation of sand more than ten li round and some twenty metres deep. A raised terrace of the period, now exposed in the middle of the city, survives, about 300 metres from north to south and some 150 metres from east to west. On this terrace archaeologists collected a great many pottery sherds and fragments of vessels in the Yue style, all identified on examination as stamped hard pottery of the late Spring and Autumn and early Warring States periods, which confirmed that these remains belong to Yue. The experts then found in Du You's Tongdian of the Tang the basis for Jinpingshan's other name, Langyashan. According to the historical records, before the Qin dynasty was founded Jinpingshan was called Qushan, also Langyashan. In the time of the First Emperor of Qin it was made Qu County, and in his thirty-fifth year (212 BC) a stone was set up there as Qin's eastern gate. In his twenty-eighth year the First Emperor also built the Langya Terrace in Shandong, to answer to the Langya settlement. Zhang Zhili and Peng Yun hold that, with the changes of place-names, the name Langyashan gradually fell out of use, and many people have therefore mistaken the place to which King Goujian of Yue moved his capital, Langyashan at Lianyungang, for the Langyashan of Jiaonan city in the Qingdao region of Shandong.
passages.no: The twenty-seventh year of Goujian's reign, 470 BC counting from his accession in 496 BC; the Shiji places his death in 465 BC. 越王孙开: read as the grandson (王孙) of a king of Yue named Kai; the words can also be read as a king of Yue named Sun Kai. 籍楚之前锋: 籍 is taken as 藉, "relying on"; the punctuation of the text sets the comma before 楚. 鲁穆柳有幽公为名，王侯自称为君: the phrase stands between Wuqiang and Zun in the line of succession, where the Yuejueshu has Zhihou and the Wu Yue Chunqiu has Yu; its wording is not explained by either text. Ivar the Boneless' analysis, from works other than the Shiji, of the end of Yue at Langya in this year: the reckoning of two hundred and twenty-four years from Goujian's hegemony, the royal lines of the Yuejueshu and the Wu Yue Chunqiu, Liu Zhao's note on the Xicen tomb, and a report on the identification of Langya with Jinpingshan at Lianyungang.

passages.title: Collected Qin Slips I: the Shuihudi bamboo slips
passages.zh: 《秦简牍合集》（一）睡虎地竹简 葉書：莊王元年。
passages.en: Collected Qin Slips I: the Shuihudi bamboo slips Chronicle: First year of King Zhuang.
passages.no: The first year of King Zhuangxiang of Qin, 249 BC, whom the Chronicle calls King Zhuang; the year is given with no entry under it. The entry for 249 BC in the Chronicle of the Shuihudi slips: the year alone, with nothing recorded under it.

passages.title: Qin slips in the Yuelu Academy collection
passages.zh: 岳麓书院藏秦简 泰上皇时内史言：西工室司寇、隐官、践更多贫不能自给粮。议：令县遣司寇入禾，其县毋（无）禾0587/329当貣者，告作所县偿及贷。西工室伐榦沮、南郑山，令沮、南郑听西工室致。其入禾者及吏移西0638/330工室。·二年曰：复用。0681/331
passages.en: Qin slips in the Yuelu Academy collection In the time of the Grand Supreme Emperor the Clerk of the Capital said: The sikou, the yinguan and those serving their geng turn at the Western Workshop are many of them poor and cannot provide their own grain. Deliberation: Let the Counties send the sikou to deliver grain; where a County has no grain to be lent, let it report to the County of the work-site for repayment and loan. The Western Workshop fells timber in the hills of Ju and Nanzheng; let Ju and Nanzheng act on the Western Workshop's requisitions. Those who deliver the grain, and the officers, are passed on to the Western Workshop. · In the second year it was said: Put back in use.
passages.no: 泰上皇, that is 太上皇, the title the First Emperor gave his father King Zhuangxiang after his death; "in the time of" the Grand Supreme Emperor is Zhuangxiang's reign, 249–247 BC, which places the statute here, at the reign's first year; the year within the reign is not given. 践更: the editors' pause marks make three groups, sikou, yinguan and men on their geng turn; Chen Wei reads 司寇、隐官践更, the sikou and yinguan on their geng turn, as in another Yuelu statute (slip 017). The editors' punctuation is kept. 议: the ruling that answers the report (言); the form of a Qin statute of this kind. 入禾: grain unhusked; the County supplies the grain its sikou will eat at the Workshop. 貣, the editors' reading 贷 kept in parentheses: 当貣者, the quantity due to be lent. 作所县: the County in which the Workshop's work-site lies. 偿及贷: as read here, the County of the work-site lends the grain and the sikou's own County repays it. 听…致: 致, the note by which an office calls for men or goods to be delivered; 听, to comply with it. 移: the forwarding of men and of the papers that go with them. ·二年曰：复用: an annotation after the scribe's dot, recording that the statute was put back in force in a second year; Chen Wei takes it as the second year of King Zheng, 245 BC. A statute of the Yuelu Academy slips (volume IV, slips 329–331; the numbers in the text are the editors' slip numbers, register number and sequence number) from the reign of King Zhuangxiang: the Clerk of the Capital's report on the poor convict labour at the Western Workshop and the ruling on it.

passages.title: Hujiacaochang Western Han slips: the Suiji (Annual Record)
passages.zh: 胡家草场西汉简牍《岁纪》 泰上皇元年。 立三年。 生始皇帝。呂不韋相......
passages.en: Hujiacaochang Western Han slips: the Suiji (Annual Record) First year of the Grand Supreme Emperor. On the throne three years. Fathered the First Emperor. Lü Buwei Chancellor......
passages.no: 泰上皇元年: the Suiji, a Han text, calls King Zhuangxiang by the title given him after his death (see §2); 249 BC. 立三年: the reign summed up at its first year, as the Suiji does for each ruler; 249–247 BC. 生始皇帝: that the king was the First Emperor's father, not that the First Emperor was born this year (the Shiji puts his birth in 259 BC). 呂不韋相: his appointment as Chancellor of State is in the Basic Annals for this year, §1. The entry goes on; the rest of it is not reproduced here. The entry for the first year of King Zhuangxiang in the Suiji (Annual Record) of the Western Han slips from Hujiacaochang, Jingzhou, which names him by his later title and sums up his reign under its first year.

passages.title: Appendix: text of the Zhanguo Zonghengjia Shu
passages.zh: 附：《戰國縱橫家書》原文 附：《贱臣筡西问秦王》： 贱臣筡西问秦王，曰：“王之外訄臣筡（愿）欲得王之倚立之閒（闲），渴（竭）腹之所闻。当今□之时，衍……巍（魏）五邦相与，陟＝若壹，为义虖（乎）？筡弗得智（知）；不为（正1）义虖（乎）？筡有（又）弗能智（知），不识吾王将可（何）以侍（待）之？”王不合（答）。筡有（又）称曰：“五邦以义来甗（献），吾王以义侍（待）之，不为义虖（乎）？（愿）吾王有以义侍（待）之者。为义者，皆欲人之以（正2）义也。”王有（又）不合（答）。筡有（又）曰：“欲有复言也，恐刀居（锯）不容于身。”王曰：“先生言也，寡人谨听。”筡曰：“今夫桀肘（纣）贵为天子，富有天下，尽已失之矣。无异故，皆以（正3）不义反为义者也。巍（魏）人与越人战宿胥之壄（野），而栖越王廥（会）稽廥纂之上；当此时，吴人侵（寝）兵立义事鬼，强为天子，吴人不侵（寝）兵立义事鬼，（正4）尽已失其先王冢庙及与大都连者。无异故，皆以不义反为义者也。今筡入，王之四竞（境）者（诸）民皆有（蚀）寒之色，窃问其故，曰：‘壹恶用兵矣。’阴晋、上雒（洛）之（正5）卒，天下之良卒也，自酆綦以来，夫斩首六矣。今出战不能胜，而内守不能箇（固），不能守其城郭而五刑传其身，而弗能佴（耻）也。无异故，皆未罢也。干将、莫冶（邪），（正6）天下之良剑也，金试□兔（？）壶（？）□□□□□……□勿绎（释）……[马录]耳，天下之良马也，重载以驰于路久而勿绎（释），骀马（正7）□至。无异故，皆未罢也。攻军杀将，王之（禄）也，者（诸）民之力也。者（诸）民绳身以断剅（头）列（裂）腹，宛取□□身以（迁）徙忧守之，此亦大过（祸）矣。万乘王所以□[于]□（背1），或欲黄金朱（珠）玉走马□猎听乐，是以闻谈说之士言攻（击）之便，得地之利，约车众者数百[乘]，而□者数十乘，齎（赍）币帛以□者（诸）侯，必旦兴师□（背2）以□边竞（境）。丈夫居军不□□□□□□□责阵卒，久者数岁，□者期年。兴而治地，地方环（圆）不□百余里，而地有不可虚，必且（迁）中□（背3）之民以实之，百姓弗安且茗，可虖（乎）？王胡不止兵毋兴令居，允其图（？）□，修其垣蘠（墙），又且相□，居得其乐而陈责皆赏。以筡之私此，此天下之良（背4）策已。黄啻□曰行年三百□椯（端）身□察乃智（知）足。今吾王之地，东南囊（？）楚而北半赵，是皆[膏]臾（腴）之地也。西尽日入之所，到无甲之□，而兵强人众莫弗（背5）智（知）已。有＝（又有）最奡、必方、婴（樱）母（梅）、橘鼬（柚）、毗（枇）杷、茈橿（姜）之林，鐘蠪胥（蹇）之州，美丹之穴，赣勒、□□、敝稯（椶）、桃支（枝）之渚，而万物无不有已。”（背6）
passages.en: Appendix: text of the Zhanguo Zonghengjia Shu Appendix: Your humble servant Tu went west to put questions to the King of Qin: Your humble servant Tu went west and put questions to the King of Qin, saying: "Your servant Tu, pressing from without, wishes to have a moment of Your Majesty's standing leisure, to pour out all that his belly holds of what he has heard. At the present □ time, Yan…… Wei and the five states are joined together and advance as one. Is this for righteousness? Tu cannot know. Is it not for righteousness? Tu again cannot know, and does not know with what my King will meet it." The King did not answer. Tu again declared: "If the five states come with righteousness to make their offer, and my King meets them with righteousness, is that not righteousness? I wish my King had the means to meet them with righteousness. Those who act for righteousness all wish others to act towards them with righteousness." The King again did not answer. Tu again said: "I wish to speak further, but fear the knife and saw will not spare my body." The King said: "Speak, sir; I listen with care." Tu said: "Now Jie and Zhou were honoured as Sons of Heaven and rich in all under Heaven, and lost it all. For no other reason: in every case they took unrighteousness for righteousness. The men of Wei fought the men of Yue in the wilds of Suxu, and perched the King of Yue on the summit of Kuaiji; at that time the men of Wu laid down their arms, established righteousness and served the spirits, and forced their way to be Son of Heaven; when the men of Wu did not lay down their arms, establish righteousness and serve the spirits, they lost it all, the tombs and temples of their former kings and whatever joined the great capital. For no other reason: in every case they took unrighteousness for righteousness. Now as Tu came in, the people within Your Majesty's four borders all had the look of hunger and cold; I privately asked the reason, and they said: 'How we hate the use of arms!' The soldiers of Yinjin and Shangluo are the finest soldiers under Heaven; since Fengqi they have taken heads six times. Now going out to battle they cannot win, and keeping guard within they cannot hold firm; they cannot hold their walls, and the five punishments pass over their bodies, yet they cannot feel it as shame. For no other reason: in every case they have never been stood down. Ganjiang and Moye are the finest swords under Heaven; tried on metal □ … □□□□□□ … never let go …; Lü'er is the finest horse under Heaven; driven on the road under heavy loads for long and never let go, a worn-out nag □ arrives. For no other reason: in every case they have never been stood down. To attack armies and kill generals is the King's gain, but it is the people's strength. The people put their bodies to the cord to have their heads cut off and their bellies ripped; … taken □□ bodies, moved away to garrison in anxious guard, this too is a great calamity. That by which a king of ten thousand chariots □ [on] □ □: some desire gold, pearls and jade, racing horses, □ hunting and listening to music, and so, hearing the persuaders tell of the ease of attack and the profit of gaining land, the great among them pledge several hundred [chariots] and the □ several tens, and carry silks and gifts to □ the Lords; and surely next morning they raise an army □ to □ the border. The men who stay in the army do not □□□□□□□ … the ranks: the longest for several years, the □ for a full year. The levy raised and the land brought under rule, a territory not □ a hundred-odd li around, and land that cannot be left empty, so that the people of the interior □ must be moved to fill it; the common people are not at ease and moreover □: can this be? Why does the King not halt the troops and raise none, and order them to stay at home, grant them their plans (?) □, repair their walls, and further □ one another, so that at home they have their joy and the arrears of levies are all rewarded? In Tu's private view, this is the finest policy under Heaven. The Yellow Emperor □ said: at three hundred years of age □, straighten the body, □ examine, and then know sufficiency. Now my King's land bags (?) Chu to the south-east and halves Zhao to the north, all of it [fertile] land. To the west it reaches where the sun goes in, to the □ of no armour; that its soldiers are strong and its people many, none does not know. It has besides forests of zui'ao, bifang, cherry and plum, orange and pomelo, loquat and purple ginger; islets of zhonglong and xujian; caves of fine cinnabar; and shoals of ganle, □□, palm and peach-branch; of the myriad things there is none it lacks."
passages.no: The text names neither the king nor the year. The excavation report (Li Tianhong and others, Wenwu 2022/3) takes the king to be King Zhuangxiang and the occasion the five-state alliance of his third year, 247 BC; the text is placed here, at the first year of the reign. The parenthesised readings are the editors'; □ marks a lost graph and …… a lost stretch; 正1 to 背6 number the lines, seven on the front of the tablet and six on the back. 王之外訄臣筡: 訄, to press; read here as the petitioner from outside the court pressing his suit. The graph after 筡 is read 愿 by the editors. 倚立之閒（闲）: the pause of a king standing, that is a short audience. 渴（竭）腹之所闻: to exhaust what his belly holds of what he has heard. 衍: unexplained; it stands where a state is expected and may be 燕 Yan, the two graphs being near in sound. Left as a name. 五邦: the five states allied against Qin; the report takes them as the Wei, Zhao, Han, Chu and Yan of Lord Xinling's alliance of 247 BC. 陟＝若壹: the ＝ is the scribe's repetition mark, 陟陟, to advance; as one. 甗, read 献 by the editors: to present terms. 刀居（锯）: the knife and the saw, the instruments of punishment. 以不义反为义: the refrain of the speech; 反 as "turned", unrighteousness turned into righteousness in their own eyes. 巍（魏）人与越人战宿胥之壄（野）: the received histories know no battle of Wei and Yue at Suxu, which lay on the Yellow River in Wei; what follows, the King of Yue perched on Kuaiji, is the Wu siege of Goujian of 494 BC. The text is left as it stands. 廥（会）稽廥纂之上: 廥纂 after 会稽 is unexplained; read as the heights of the mountain. 侵, read 寝 by the editors: 寝兵, to lay arms to rest. 强为天子: Wu's claim to lead the Lords under King Fuchai, as at the meeting of Huangchi. 及与大都连者: the lands adjoining the great capital. 有（蚀）寒之色: the editors read the graph as 蚀 and take the phrase as the look of gaunt hunger and cold; Wang Ning would read 饥 outright. 壹恶用兵矣: 壹 as the intensifier, how greatly. 酆綦: not identified; the readings proposed are 逢忌, the marsh of Fengji near Daliang (Lin Xiaoyang), and 豐析 (Xie Minghong). Left as a name. 斩首六矣: the unit of the six is not given; six campaigns, or six (tens of thousands of) heads. 佴, read 耻 by the editors. 皆未罢也: 罢, to be released from service; the soldiers have never been relieved. The sentence recurs as a refrain of the swords and the horse. 金试□兔（？）壶（？）□□□□□……□勿绎（释）: the sentence on the swords is largely lost; 绎, read 释 by the editors, to let go, as of the horse below. 骀马: a broken-down horse; the finest horse, never rested, ends a nag. 王之（禄）也: the editors read the graph as 禄, emolument. 绳身: literally to cord the body; read as to bind themselves to the service that costs them 断剅（头）列（裂）腹, heads cut off and bellies ripped. 宛取□□身以（迁）徙忧守之: the graph read 迁 by the editors; the people moved to hold new land in anxious guard. 约车众者数百[乘]: 乘 supplied by the editors in brackets; 约车, to bind oneself to furnish chariots. 责阵卒: the sense of the sentence is lost with its seven graphs. 兴而治地，地方环（圆）不□百余里: the land won by a campaign, a hundred-odd li round, must be peopled from the interior (中□之民). 且茗: 茗 unexplained. 允其图（？）□: the editors' reading, queried by them. 陈责皆赏: 陈责, old debts or arrears; 赏 as read, rewarded, or remitted. 黄啻□曰行年三百□椯（端）身□察乃智（知）足: 黄啻 is the Yellow Emperor (啻 for 帝); the saying is broken by two lost graphs; 椯 read 端 by the editors. 东南囊（？）楚而北半赵: the editors query 囊; Qin's land enclosing Chu to the south-east and taking half of Zhao to the north, after the fall of Ying in 278 BC and Changping in 260 BC. 膏 supplied by the editors in brackets. 到无甲之□: the far west where no armour is worn; the graph lost. 最奡: the editors read 奡 as 豪, the porcupine; Wang Ning reads 獒, a dog; Fang Yong reads the graph as 戛, 最戛 for 丛棘, thickets of jujube; Cai Wei reads 獿 and Xie Minghong 狙猱, the macaque. Romanised. 必方: the editors read 苾芳, fragrant plants, and note the bird 畢方; Fang Yong reads 枋, a tree. Romanised. 婴（樱）母（梅）: the editors' reading; Wang Ning reads 鹦鹉, the parrot, as the Shijing commentary writes it. 鐘蠪胥（蹇）之州: 鐘蠪 read 籦籠, a bamboo (Bing Shangbai); 胥蹇 likewise a bamboo; 州 as islet. 赣勒: read 瑊玏, a stone like jade (Cai Wei). Romanised. 敝稯（椶）、桃支（枝）: 敝椶 the palm (栟櫚), 桃枝 a bamboo. A persuasion on a wooden tablet (觚) from tomb M274 at Zhengjiahu, Yunmeng, Hubei, inscribed in seven lines on the front and six on the back and published in Wenwu 2022/3: a persuader named Tu urges a King of Qin to lay down arms, and is twice met with silence. The text, unknown to the received literature, names neither the king nor the year; the excavation report takes the king to be King Zhuangxiang and the occasion the five-state alliance of 247 BC. It is placed here with the appended texts of the Warring States persuaders.

passages.title: Shiji I: Basic Annals
passages.zh: 史记（一：本纪） 秦本纪：二年，使蒙骜攻赵，定太原。
passages.en: Shiji I: Basic Annals Basic Annals of Qin: In the second year he sent Meng Ao to attack Zhao and settled Taiyuan.
passages.no: The second year of King Zhuangxiang of Qin, 248 BC; the king is the subject. 定太原: the Tables and the Hereditary Houses (§2, §3) give the campaign as the taking of Yuci and thirty-seven cities, and the Hereditary House of Yan adds that Qin set up Taiyuan Commandery. The Basic Annals of Qin for the second year of King Zhuangxiang: Meng Ao's campaign against Zhao and the settling of Taiyuan.

passages.title: Shiji II: Tables
passages.zh: 史记（二：表） 秦：蒙驚擊趙榆次、新城、狼孟， 得三十七城。 日蝕。 楚：春申君徙封於吳。
passages.en: Shiji II: Tables Qin: Meng Ao struck Zhao's Yuci, Xincheng and Langmeng, and took thirty-seven Fortresses. Eclipse of the sun. Chu: Lord Chunshen's fief was moved to Wu.
passages.no: 蒙驚: the three-commentary edition reads 蒙驁, Meng Ao, as the Basic Annals (§1). The Zhengyi on the Basic Annals (案：取三十七城，并、代、朔三州之地矣): the thirty-seven Fortresses are the lands of the three States of Bingzhou, Daizhou and Shuozhou, in the names of the Tang; the Hereditary Houses (§3) count them as taken at Yuci. 日蝕: entered in the Table's Qin column for the year. 徙封於吳: from the twelve Counties north of the Huai to the old seat of Wu, as the Biography of Lord Chunshen (§4) tells. The row of the Table of the Six States for this year: the entries for Qin and Chu.

passages.title: Shiji III: Hereditary Houses
passages.zh: 史记（三：世家） 燕召公世家：七年，秦拔赵榆次三十七城，秦置大原郡。 赵世家：十八年，延陵钧率师从相国信平君助魏攻燕。秦拔我榆次三十七城。
passages.en: Shiji III: Hereditary Houses Hereditary House of Duke Shao of Yan: In the seventh year, Qin took Zhao's Yuci and thirty-seven Fortresses; Qin set up Taiyuan Commandery. Hereditary House of Zhao: In the eighteenth year, Yanling Jun led an army under the Chancellor of State Lord Xinping to help Wei attack Yan. Qin took our Yuci and thirty-seven Fortresses.
passages.no: The seventh year of King Xi of Yan, 248 BC. 榆次三十七城: the thirty-seven Fortresses of the Table's entry (§2), Yuci the first of them. 大原 is written for 太原. The Basic Annals of Qin put the founding of Taiyuan Commandery in the next year, the king's third. The eighteenth year of King Xiaocheng of Zhao, 248 BC. Lian Po, Acting Chancellor of State since the fifteenth year (251 BC) in this Hereditary House, here Chancellor of State. The Hereditary Houses of Yan and of Zhao for this year: Qin's taking of Yuci and thirty-seven Fortresses, told from both sides, and Zhao's army sent to help Wei against Yan.

passages.title: Shiji IV: Biographies
passages.zh: 史记（四：列传） 春申君列传：考烈王元年，以黄歇为相，封为春申君，赐淮北地十二县。後十五岁，黄歇言之楚王曰：“淮北地边齐，其事急，请以为郡便。”因并献淮北十二县。请封於江东。考烈王许之。春申君因城故吴墟，以自为都邑。
passages.en: Shiji IV: Biographies Biography of Lord Chunshen: In the first year of King Kaolie he made Huang Xie Chancellor, enfeoffed him as Lord Chunshen, and granted him twelve Counties of the land north of the Huai. Fifteen years later Huang Xie said to the King of Chu: "The land north of the Huai borders Qi, and its affairs are pressing; it would be better made a Commandery." And he gave back the twelve Counties north of the Huai, asking to be enfeoffed in Jiangdong. King Kaolie consented. Lord Chunshen accordingly fortified the old ruins of Wu and made them his seat.
passages.no: 262 BC. The passage is the one already given in the Biography for 255 BC (§4), repeated here for the move it dates. The fifteenth year of King Kaolie, 248 BC, where the Table (§2) enters the move of the fief to Wu. The passage of the Biography of Lord Chunshen on his fief: the twelve Counties north of the Huai given up for Jiangdong, fifteen years after his enfeoffment, and the old seat of Wu made his own.

passages.title: Shiji V: Biographies
passages.zh: 史记（五：列传） 蒙恬列传：二年，蒙骜攻赵，取三十七城。
passages.en: Shiji V: Biographies Biography of Meng Tian: In the second year Meng Ao attacked Zhao and took thirty-seven Fortresses.
passages.no: The second year of King Zhuangxiang of Qin, 248 BC; the Biography continues the sentence begun under the first year (249 BC, §5). The Biography of Meng Tian for this year: his grandfather Meng Ao's campaign against Zhao and the thirty-seven Fortresses.

passages.title: Ivar the Boneless' commentary and analysis I
passages.zh: 无骨论点补充（以及辨析）一 秦将井忌助赵攻燕，拔二城。 辨析：事見《戰國縱橫家書》，但是時間不詳： 二十五、李园谓辛梧章 秦使辛梧据粱（梁），合秦粱（梁）而攻楚。李园忧之。兵未出，谓辛梧：“以秦之强，有两端之劲，东面而伐楚。于臣也，楚不侍（待）伐割挚马免而西走，秦余（与）楚为上交，秦祸案环（还）中粱（梁）矣。将军必逐于粱（梁），恐诛于秦。 将军不见井忌乎？为秦据赵而攻燕，拔二城。燕使蔡鸟股符〓去壁，奸（间）赵入秦，以河间十城封秦相文信侯。文信侯弗敢受，曰：‘我无功。’ 蔡鸟明日见，带长剑，举其末，视视（示）文信侯曰：‘君曰我无功，君无功，胡不解君之玺，以佩蒙敖（骜）、王〓也？秦王以君为贤，故加君二人之上。今燕献地。此非秦之地也。君弗受，不忠。’文信侯敬若（诺）。言之秦王，秦王令受之。余（与）燕为上交，秦祸案环（还）归于赵矣。秦大举兵东面而赍赵，言毋攻燕。以秦之强，有燕之怒，割勺（赵）必深。赵不能听，逐井忌，诛于秦。今臣窃为将军私计，不如少案（按）之，毋庸出兵，秦未得志于楚，必重粱（梁），粱（梁）未得志于楚，必重秦，是将军两重。天下人无不死者，久者寿。愿将军之察之也。粱（梁）兵未出，楚见粱（梁）之未出兵也，走秦必缓。秦王怒于楚之缓也，怨必深。是将军有（又）重矣。”粱（梁）兵果六月乃出。
passages.en: Ivar the Boneless' commentary and analysis I The Qin general Jing Ji helped Zhao attack Yan and took two Fortresses. Analysis: the matter is seen in the Zhanguo Zonghengjia Shu, but the time is not known: Chapter 25, Li Yuan speaks to Xin Wu Qin sent Xin Wu to hold Liang, to join Qin and Liang in an attack on Chu. Li Yuan was troubled by this. Before the troops had set out he said to Xin Wu: "With Qin's strength and the force of two arms, you face east and attack Chu. As your servant sees it, Chu will not wait to be attacked: it will cede land and bring gifts and hurry west, Qin and Chu will become the closest of allies, and Qin's blow will then fall back upon Liang. The General will surely be driven out of Liang, and I fear put to death by Qin. Has the General not seen the case of Jing Ji? On Qin's behalf he held Zhao and attacked Yan, taking two Fortresses. Yan sent Cai Niao, who with a tally made his way out through the ramparts, passed secretly through Zhao into Qin and offered the ten Fortresses of Hejian as a fief to the Chancellor of Qin, Marquis Wenxin. Marquis Wenxin did not dare accept, saying: 'I have no merit.' The next day Cai Niao came to see him wearing a long sword, raised its point and showed it to Marquis Wenxin, saying: 'You say "I have no merit". If you have no merit, why not untie your seal and hang it on Meng Ao or Wang 〓? The King of Qin holds you worthy, and so has set you above those two. Now Yan offers land; this is not Qin's land. If you do not accept it, you are disloyal.' Marquis Wenxin respectfully agreed. He spoke of it to the King of Qin, and the King of Qin ordered him to accept. Qin became Yan's closest ally, and Qin's blow then turned back upon Zhao. Qin raised a great army, faced east and bore down on Zhao, declaring that Yan was not to be attacked. With Qin's strength and Yan's anger, the cutting of Zhao was bound to go deep. Zhao could not bear it; it drove out Jing Ji, and he was put to death by Qin. Now, if your servant may privately plan for the General: better to hold back a little and not send out the troops. So long as Qin has not had its way with Chu, it must value Liang; so long as Liang has not had its way with Chu, it must value Qin — thus the General is valued on both sides. No man under Heaven escapes death; he who lasts long lives long. I wish the General to consider it. While Liang's troops have not set out, Chu, seeing that Liang has not sent out its troops, will be slow to hurry to Qin. The King of Qin, angered at Chu's slowness, will resent it deeply; and so the General is valued still more." Liang's troops did indeed set out only after six months.
passages.no: The chapter is the one appended under 256 BC (§6), where its translation and notes first appear; it is repeated here as the compiler adduces it for Jing Ji's campaign. The two graphs the manuscript leaves illegible are given as 〓, as there. In the appended chapter the characters in parentheses are the editors' readings of the manuscript graphs before them (粱 read 梁, 侍 read 待, and so on); the translation follows the readings. 割挚马免: no published reading of the phrase was found; 挚 is taken as 贽, "gifts", and the rendering is approximate. 股符〓去壁: 〓 marks a graph illegible in the manuscript. The Wikisource transcription of the text reads 股符胠壁, 胠 "to break open" and 壁 "rampart"; 股 is unexplained, and the rendering is tentative. 文信侯: Lü Buwei, under the title the Zhanguo Zonghengjia Shu gives him. 王〓: the graph after 王 is illegible in the manuscript. 赍赵 (齎趙 in the transcription): 齎 is probably a loan for 挤, "to press"; the reading is not settled. Ivar the Boneless' commentary on the year: Jing Ji's campaign for Zhao against Yan, with chapter 25 of the Zhanguo Zonghengjia Shu adduced for it, its date unknown.

passages.title: Ivar the Boneless' commentary and analysis II
passages.zh: 无骨论点补充（以及辨析）二 燕献河间十城于秦相吕不韦，秦庄襄王令吕不韦受地，兴兵胁迫赵国“毋攻燕”，赵孝成王不听。 辨析：事見《戰國縱橫家書》，但是時間不詳： 二十五、李园谓辛梧章（左側） 赵相邦春平侯、平国君先后入秦，被秦庄襄王留为人质。 辨析：此應根據《戰國策·秦召春平侯》，但原文並未說明具體時間。 又：《論春平侯及其相關問題》：平都侯当即铍铭所见的“平国君”。文献以“都”换“国”字的情况，跟文献所见的“信平君”、“建信君”之“信”，铍铭都写作“躬(躬)”类似。 又：《史記·趙世家》把此事歸在趙悼襄王二年。 赵孝成王命信平君廉颇担任相邦。 辨析：此應根據《史記·趙世家》，廉颇在趙孝成王十五年已擔任守相。
passages.en: Ivar the Boneless' commentary and analysis II Yan offered the ten Fortresses of Hejian to the Chancellor of Qin, Lü Buwei; King Zhuangxiang of Qin ordered Lü Buwei to accept the land, and raised troops to press Zhao "not to attack Yan"; King Xiaocheng of Zhao did not comply. Analysis: the matter is seen in the Zhanguo Zonghengjia Shu, but the time is not known: Chapter 25, Li Yuan speaks to Xin Wu (at left) Zhao's Chancellor of State Marquis Chunping and Lord Pingguo went into Qin one after the other and were kept by King Zhuangxiang of Qin as hostages. Analysis: this should rest on the Zhanguoce, "Qin summons Marquis Chunping", but the original text does not give the time. Further, from "On Marquis Chunping and the questions connected with him": Marquis Pingdu must be the "Lord Pingguo" seen in the pi-blade inscriptions. The texts' putting 都 for 国 is like the 信 of the texts' "Lord Xinping" and "Lord Jianxin", which the pi inscriptions all write 躬 (躬). Further: the Hereditary House of Zhao in the Shiji places this matter in the second year of King Daoxiang of Zhao. King Xiaocheng of Zhao appointed Lord Xinping, Lian Po, Chancellor of State. Analysis: this should rest on the Hereditary House of Zhao in the Shiji, where Lian Po was already Acting Chancellor in the fifteenth year of King Xiaocheng.
passages.no: 左側: the chapter is appended in the compiler's first column of commentary, §6. 秦召春平侯: a chapter of the Strategies of Qin in the Zhanguoce. 論春平侯及其相關問題: the modern study the compiler cites, on the Zhao pi-blade inscriptions. 躬(躬): the inscriptional graph and its reading, as the compiler writes them. 243 BC. 251 BC; see the Hereditary House of Zhao for that year (251 BC, §3). Ivar the Boneless' second column of commentary on the year: Yan's gift of Hejian to Lü Buwei, the Zhao ministers held in Qin as hostages, and Lian Po's chancellorship, each with his analysis of the source and its date.

passages.title: Collected Qin Slips I: the Shuihudi bamboo slips
passages.zh: 《秦简牍合集》（一）睡虎地竹简 葉書：莊王二年。
passages.en: Collected Qin Slips I: the Shuihudi bamboo slips Chronicle: Second year of King Zhuang.
passages.no: The second year of King Zhuangxiang of Qin, 248 BC, whom the Chronicle calls King Zhuang; the year is given with no entry under it. The entry for 248 BC in the Chronicle of the Shuihudi slips: the year alone, with nothing recorded under it.

passages.title: Shiji I: Basic Annals
passages.zh: 史记（一：本纪） 秦本纪：三年，蒙骜攻魏高都、汲，拔之。攻赵榆次、新城、狼孟，取三十七城。四月日食。王龁攻上党。初置太原郡。魏将无忌率五国兵击秦，秦却于河外。蒙骜败，解而去。五月丙午，庄襄王卒，子政立，是为秦始皇帝。
passages.en: Shiji I: Basic Annals Basic Annals of Qin: In the third year Meng Ao attacked Wei's Gaodu and Ji and took them. He attacked Zhao's Yuci, Xincheng and Langmeng and took thirty-seven Fortresses. In April there was an eclipse of the sun. Wang He attacked Shangdang. Taiyuan Commandery was established for the first time. The Wei general Wuji led the troops of five states against Qin, and Qin fell back to Hewai. Meng Ao was defeated, broke off and withdrew. In May, on the day Bingwu, King Zhuangxiang died, and his son Zheng was set up: this was the First Emperor of Qin.
passages.no: The third year of King Zhuangxiang of Qin, 247 BC. The Jijie cites Xu Guang: one text has 波 for 汲, Bo County being also in Henei. The Zhengyi cites the Kuodizhi: the old city of Gaodu is Zezhou; the old city of Ji lies twenty-five li south-west of the Ji County governed from Weizhou. The Zhengyi cites the Kuodizhi: Yuci is a County of Bingzhou, the ancient Yuci; Xincheng, also called Xiaopingcheng, lies forty-seven li south-west of Shanyang County in Shuozhou; the old city of Langmeng twenty-six li north-east of Yangqu County in Bingzhou. The Table and the Hereditary Houses enter the campaign under the previous year (248 BC, §2, §3). The Zhengyi: the thirty-seven Fortresses are the lands of the three States of Bingzhou, Daizhou and Shuozhou, in the names of the Tang. 四月日食: the Table enters an eclipse under the previous year (248 BC, §2). 王龁: the Basic Annals' writing of the general whom the Table (§2) and the Suiji call 王齮, Wang Yi; the two are taken as one man. The Zhengyi: Shangdang had again turned against Qin, hence the attack. The Zhengyi: all north of Shangdang is Taiyuan land, that is the thirty-seven Fortresses above. The Hereditary House of Yan puts the founding under the previous year (248 BC, §3). The Zhengyi: Wuji is Lord Xinling; he led the troops of Yan, Zhao, Han, Chu and Wei against Qin. The Zhengyi: Meng Ao, beaten by the five states' troops, broke off and fell back to Hewai, the States of Shanzhou and Huazhou in the names of the Tang. 子政: Ying Zheng, King of Qin from this accession; the Basic Annals name him by the imperial title he took later. The Basic Annals of Qin for the third and last year of King Zhuangxiang: Meng Ao's campaigns in Wei and Zhao, the founding of Taiyuan Commandery, the five-state army under Lord Xinling that drove Qin back to Hewai, and the king's death in May and the accession of his son Zheng.

passages.title: Shiji II: Tables
passages.zh: 史记（二：表） 秦：王齮擊上黨。初置太原郡。 魏公子無忌率五國卻我軍河外，蒙驁解去。 魏：無忌率五國兵敗秦軍河外。 韓：秦拔我上黨。
passages.en: Shiji II: Tables Qin: Wang Yi struck Shangdang. Taiyuan Commandery was established for the first time. Prince Wuji of Wei led five states and drove our army back at Hewai; Meng Ao broke off and withdrew. Wei: Wuji led the troops of five states and defeated the Qin army at Hewai. Han: Qin took our Shangdang.
passages.no: 王齮: the Basic Annals (§1) write 王龁 for the same general. The Zhengyi on the Basic Annals names them: Yan, Zhao, Han, Chu and Wei (§1). The Table's second Qin line and its Wei line record the same battle from the two sides. The row of the Table of the Six States for this year: the entries for Qin, Wei and Han.

passages.title: Shiji III: Hereditary Houses
passages.zh: 史记（三：世家） 楚世家：十六年，秦庄襄王卒，秦王赵政立。 赵世家：十九年，赵与燕易土：以龙兑、汾门、临乐与燕；燕以葛、武阳、平舒与赵。 魏世家：三十年，无忌归魏，率五国兵攻秦，败之河外，走蒙骜。魏太子增质於秦，秦怒，欲囚魏太子增。或为增谓秦王曰：“公孙喜固谓魏相曰‘请以魏疾击秦，秦王怒，必囚增。魏王又怒，击秦，秦必伤’。今王囚增，是喜之计中也。故不若贵增而合魏，以疑之於齐、韩。”秦乃止增。 韩世家：二十六年，秦悉拔我上党。
passages.en: Shiji III: Hereditary Houses Hereditary House of Chu: In the sixteenth year, King Zhuangxiang of Qin died, and the King of Qin, Zhao Zheng, was set up. Hereditary House of Zhao: In the nineteenth year, Zhao and Yan exchanged land: Zhao gave Longdui, Fenmen and Linle to Yan, and Yan gave Ge, Wuyang and Pingshu to Zhao. Hereditary House of Wei: In the thirtieth year, Wuji returned to Wei, led the troops of five states to attack Qin, defeated them at Hewai and put Meng Ao to flight. The Heir Apparent of Wei, Zeng, was a hostage in Qin; Qin was angered and wished to imprison the Heir Apparent of Wei, Zeng. Someone said to the King of Qin on Zeng's behalf: "Gongsun Xi firmly told the Chancellor of Wei: 'Let Wei attack Qin hard; the King of Qin will be angered and will surely imprison Zeng. The King of Wei will be angered in turn and attack Qin, and Qin will surely be hurt.' Now if the King imprisons Zeng, Xi's plan has hit its mark. So it is better to honour Zeng and ally with Wei, so as to make Qi and Han suspicious of it." Qin thereupon let Zeng be. Hereditary House of Han: In the twenty-sixth year, Qin took all our Shangdang.
passages.no: The sixteenth year of King Kaolie of Chu, 247 BC. 赵政: the First Emperor by his clan name Zhao, as the Chu house writes him; born in Zhao, he was of the Zhao clan of the Ying line. The nineteenth year of King Xiaocheng of Zhao, 247 BC. 易土: the Suoyin gives the pronunciation of 易 as that of 亦 and glosses it as exchanging Counties with Yan. The commentaries' placing of the six towns is in their entries. The thirtieth year of King Anxi of Wei, 247 BC. The Prince's return and the battle are told at length in his Biography, 256 BC §4. 或: the Suoyin notes that the Zhanguoce has Su Qin speaking for Prince Zeng. 公孙喜: the Suoyin notes that the Zhanguoce writes Gongsun Yan 公孙衍. The twenty-sixth year of King Huanhui of Han, 247 BC. The Hereditary Houses of Chu, Zhao, Wei and Han for this year: the accession of Zhao Zheng, the exchange of six towns between Zhao and Yan, Wuji's victory at Hewai and the Wei hostage Zeng spared by Qin, and the loss of Han's Shangdang.

passages.title: Shiji IV: Biographies
passages.zh: 史记（四：列传） 魏公子列传：魏王怒公子之盗其兵符，矫杀晋鄙，公子亦自知也。已卻秦存赵，使将将其军归魏，而公子独与客留赵。赵孝成王德公子之矫夺晋鄙兵而存赵，乃与平原君计，以五城封公子。公子闻之，意骄矜而有自功之色。客有说公子曰：“物有不可忘，或有不可不忘。夫人有德於公子，公子不可忘也；公子有德於人，原公子忘之也。且矫魏王令，夺晋鄙兵以救赵，於赵则有功矣，於魏则未为忠臣也。公子乃自骄而功之，窃为公子不取也。”於是公子立自责，似若无所容者。赵王埽除自迎，执主人之礼，引公子就西阶。公子侧行辞让，从东阶上。自言罪过，以负於魏，无功於赵。赵王侍酒至暮，口不忍献五城，以公子退让也。公子竟留赵。赵王以鄗为公子汤沐邑，魏亦复以信陵奉公子。公子留赵。 公子闻赵有处士毛公藏於博徒，薛公藏於卖浆家，公子欲见两人，两人自匿不肯见公子。公子闻所在，乃间步往从此两人游，甚欢。平原君闻之，谓其夫人曰：“始吾闻夫人弟公子天下无双，今吾闻之，乃妄从博徒卖浆者游，公子妄人耳。”夫人以告公子。公子乃谢夫人去，曰：“始吾闻平原君贤，故负魏王而救赵，以称平原君。平原君之游，徒豪举耳，不求士也。无忌自在大梁时，常闻此两人贤，至赵，恐不得见。以无忌从之游，尚恐其不我欲也，今平原君乃以为羞，其不足从游。”乃装为去。夫人具以语平原君。平原君乃免冠谢，固留公子。平原君门下闻之，半去平原君归公子，天下士复往归公子，公子倾平原君客。 公子留赵十年不归。秦闻公子在赵，日夜出兵东伐魏。魏王患之，使使往请公子。公子恐其怒之，乃诫门下：“有敢为魏王使通者，死。”宾客皆背魏之赵，莫敢劝公子归。毛公、薛公两人往见公子曰：“公子所以重於赵，名闻诸侯者，徒以有魏也。今秦攻魏，魏急而公子不恤，使秦破大梁而夷先王之宗庙，公子当何面目立天下乎？”语未及卒，公子立变色，告车趣驾归救魏。 魏王见公子，相与泣，而以上将军印授公子，公子遂将。魏安釐王三十年，公子使使遍告诸侯。诸侯闻公子将，各遣将将兵救魏。公子率五国之兵破秦军於河外，走蒙骜。遂乘胜逐秦军至函谷关，抑秦兵，秦兵不敢出。当是时，公子威振天下，诸侯之客进兵法，公子皆名之，故世俗称魏公子兵法。 秦王患之，乃行金万斤於魏，求晋鄙客，令毁公子於魏王曰：“公子亡在外十年矣，今为魏将，诸侯将皆属，诸侯徒闻魏公子，不闻魏王。公子亦欲因此时定南面而王，诸侯畏公子之威，方欲共立之。”秦数使反间，伪贺公子得立为魏王未也。魏王日闻其毁，不能不信，後果使人代公子将。公子自知再以毁废，乃谢病不朝，与宾客为长夜饮，饮醇酒，多近妇女。日夜为乐饮者四岁，竟病酒而卒。其岁，魏安釐王亦薨。 秦闻公子死，使蒙骜攻魏，拔二十城，初置东郡。其後秦稍蚕食魏，十八岁而虏魏王，屠大梁。 高祖始微少时，数闻公子贤。及即天子位，每过大梁，常祠公子。高祖十二年，从击黥布还，为公子置守冢五家，世世岁以四时奉祠公子。 太史公曰：吾过大梁之墟，求问其所谓夷门。夷门者，城之东门也。天下诸公子亦有喜士者矣，然信陵君之接岩穴隐者，不耻下交，有以也。名冠诸侯，不虚耳。高祖每过之而令民奉祠不绝也。
passages.en: Shiji IV: Biographies Biography of the Prince of Wei: The King of Wei was angry that the Prince had stolen his army tally and killed Jin Bi under a feigned command, and the Prince knew it himself. Having driven back Qin and preserved Zhao, he had a general lead his army back to Wei, while the Prince alone stayed in Zhao with his retainers. King Xiaocheng of Zhao, grateful to the Prince for seizing Jin Bi's army under a feigned command and preserving Zhao, planned with Lord Pingyuan to enfeoff the Prince with five Fortresses. When the Prince heard of it, his mind grew proud and he wore the look of one who takes credit for his deed. One of his retainers said to the Prince: "There are things that must not be forgotten, and things that must not be remembered. When another has done the Prince a kindness, the Prince must not forget it; when the Prince has done another a kindness, I would have the Prince forget it. Moreover, to feign the King of Wei's command and seize Jin Bi's army to relieve Zhao was a service to Zhao, but towards Wei it was not the act of a loyal subject. For the Prince to grow proud and take credit for it — I privately think the Prince should not." At this the Prince at once reproached himself, as if there were nowhere he could hide. The King of Zhao swept the way and came to meet him in person, performed the rites of a host, and led the Prince towards the western steps. The Prince stepped aside in refusal and went up by the eastern steps. He declared his own fault: he had failed Wei and done no service to Zhao. The King of Zhao kept him at wine until dusk, and could not bring himself to offer the five Fortresses, because of the Prince's self-abasement. In the end the Prince stayed in Zhao. The King of Zhao gave the Prince Hao as his private estate, and Wei too restored Xinling for the Prince's support. The Prince remained in Zhao.
